title: Op-amps I: inverting and non-inverting amplifiers
goal: Build an inverting amplifier with an LM741, confirm its gain and phase, find where it clips, and see how the gain–bandwidth product limits its bandwidth.
theory: With negative feedback an op-amp drives its output until its two inputs are at the same voltage. In the inverting amplifier IN+ is grounded, so IN− is a virtual ground: the input current V_in/R_in must all flow through R_f, giving V_out = −(R_f/R_in)·V_in.
The non-inverting amplifier (signal into IN+, R_in from IN− to ground) has gain 1 + R_f/R_in and no inversion.

The output cannot go past its supply rails; a 741 on ±12 V clips about 1.5 V inside them. Its gain–bandwidth product is about 1 MHz, so a closed-loop noise gain of 1 + R_f/R_in = 11 leaves a bandwidth near 1 MHz/11 ≈ 91 kHz. The slew rate (0.5 V/µs) limits large fast signals.

prelab.label: Gain of the inverting amplifier, R_in = 10 kΩ, R_f = 100 kΩ
Output Vpp for a 0.5 Vpp input
Input Vpp at which the output starts to clip (±10.5 V)

procedure: Load the reference build: LM741 across the centre gap (U1), ±12 V from the triple supply, R_in = RIN, R_f = RF. The generator gives 0.5 Vpp at 1 kHz.
Scope CH1 on the input (column 15), CH2 on the output (column 22). Measure both Vpp and confirm the 180° inversion.
Raise the generator amplitude until the output flattens at the top and bottom: that is saturation. Note the input Vpp.
Bench → Bode from i15 to d22 (10 Hz – 1 MHz). Read the mid-band gain in dB and the −3 dB frequency; compare with GBW/(1 + R_f/R_in).
Rewire as a non-inverting amplifier (generator into IN+, RIN from IN− to ground) and measure the new gain.
